Master Solved Algorithms

TITLE

Step-by-Step Solved Algorithms Guide (Unit 1 to Unit 7)​

EXAM MASTER STRATEGY

This guide provides complete, step-by-step numerical solutions accompanied by visual graphs, state-space trees, and automata for every algorithm across all 7 units of Design and Analysis of Algorithms. Every step is broken down with one calculation per line to make revision easy and exam-ready.

Unit - 1

Basics of Algorithms and Mathematics​

1.1 Karatsuba Integer Multiplication​

1.1.1 Concept​

  • Standard grade-school multiplication takes 444 sub-multiplications for 222-digit halves.
  • Karatsuba's algorithm performs only 333 recursive multiplications.
  • The cross-term (ad+bc)(ad + bc)(ad+bc) is obtained via the algebraic identity: Middle=(a+b)(c+d)−ac−bd\text{Middle} = (a + b)(c + d) - ac - bdMiddle=(a+b)(c+d)−ac−bd

1.1.2 Problem Statement & Input​

  • Multiply two 444-digit integers:
    • X=1234X = 1234X=1234
    • Y=5678Y = 5678Y=5678
  • Number of digits: n=4n = 4n=4
  • Half-length: m=⌈n/2⌉=2m = \lceil n / 2 \rceil = 2m=⌈n/2⌉=2

1.1.3 Step-by-Step Solved Walkthrough​

Step 1: Split the Numbers into Halves​
  • Number XXX:
    • High half: a=⌊1234/102⌋=12a = \lfloor 1234 / 10^2 \rfloor = 12a=⌊1234/102⌋=12
    • Low half: b=1234(mod102)=34b = 1234 \pmod{10^2} = 34b=1234(mod102)=34
  • Number YYY:
    • High half: c=⌊5678/102⌋=56c = \lfloor 5678 / 10^2 \rfloor = 56c=⌊5678/102⌋=56
    • Low half: d=5678(mod102)=78d = 5678 \pmod{10^2} = 78d=5678(mod102)=78
Step 2: Compute the Three Primary Products​

  • Product 1 (High halves product): p1=a×cp_1 = a \times cp1​=a×c p1=12×56p_1 = 12 \times 56p1​=12×56 p1=672p_1 = 672p1​=672

  • Product 2 (Low halves product): p2=b×dp_2 = b \times dp2​=b×d p2=34×78p_2 = 34 \times 78p2​=34×78 p2=2652p_2 = 2652p2​=2652

  • Product 3 (Sum of halves product): p3=(a+b)×(c+d)p_3 = (a + b) \times (c + d)p3​=(a+b)×(c+d) a+b=12+34=46a + b = 12 + 34 = 46a+b=12+34=46 c+d=56+78=134c + d = 56 + 78 = 134c+d=56+78=134 p3=46×134p_3 = 46 \times 134p3​=46×134 p3=6164p_3 = 6164p3​=6164

Step 3: Compute the Middle Cross-Term​
  • Cross-term formula: Middle=p3−p1−p2\text{Middle} = p_3 - p_1 - p_2Middle=p3​−p1​−p2​ Middle=6164−672−2652\text{Middle} = 6164 - 672 - 2652Middle=6164−672−2652 Middle=6164−3324\text{Middle} = 6164 - 3324Middle=6164−3324 Middle=2840\text{Middle} = 2840Middle=2840
Step 4: Assemble the Final Product​
  • Standard assembly formula: Result=p1⋅102m+Middle⋅10m+p2\text{Result} = p_1 \cdot 10^{2m} + \text{Middle} \cdot 10^m + p_2Result=p1​⋅102m+Middle⋅10m+p2​
  • Substituting values: Term1=672×104=6,720,000\text{Term}_1 = 672 \times 10^4 = 6,720,000Term1​=672×104=6,720,000 Term2=2840×102=284,000\text{Term}_2 = 2840 \times 10^2 = 284,000Term2​=2840×102=284,000 Term3=2652\text{Term}_3 = 2652Term3​=2652
  • Summation: Result=6,720,000+284,000+2,652\text{Result} = 6,720,000 + 284,000 + 2,652Result=6,720,000+284,000+2,652 Result=7,006,652\text{Result} = 7,006,652Result=7,006,652
Step 5: Verification​
  • Direct multiplication: 1234×5678=7,006,6521234 \times 5678 = 7,006,6521234×5678=7,006,652
  • The result matches exactly.

1.1.4 Complexity Analysis​

  • Recurrence relation: T(n)=3T(n/2)+O(n)T(n) = 3T(n/2) + O(n)T(n)=3T(n/2)+O(n)
  • By Master Theorem: a=3,b=2,log⁡23≈1.585a = 3, \quad b = 2, \quad \log_2 3 \approx 1.585a=3,b=2,log2​3≈1.585
  • Time Complexity: Θ(nlog⁡23)≈O(n1.585)\Theta(n^{\log_2 3}) \approx \mathbf{O(n^{1.585})}Θ(nlog2​3)≈O(n1.585)
  • Space Complexity: O(n)\mathbf{O(n)}O(n) due to recursive call stack.

1.3 Substitution Method (Mathematical Induction)​

1.3.1 Problem Definition​

  • Solve the recurrence: T(n)=2T(⌊n/2⌋)+nT(n) = 2T(\lfloor n/2 \rfloor) + nT(n)=2T(⌊n/2⌋)+n
  • Base case: T(1)=1T(1) = 1T(1)=1
  • Target:
    • Prove that T(n)=O(nlog⁡2n)T(n) = O(n \log_2 n)T(n)=O(nlog2​n).

1.3.2 Inductive Hypothesis​

  • Assume that for all integers k<nk < nk<n: T(k)≤c⋅klog⁡2kT(k) \le c \cdot k \log_2 kT(k)≤c⋅klog2​k
  • Constant c>0c > 0c>0 will be determined.

1.3.3 Inductive Step Proof​

  • Start with the recurrence definition: T(n)=2T(n/2)+nT(n) = 2T(n/2) + nT(n)=2T(n/2)+n
  • Substitute the hypothesis for k=n/2k = n/2k=n/2: T(n)≤2[c(n2)log⁡2(n2)]+nT(n) \le 2 \left[ c \left(\frac{n}{2}\right) \log_2\left(\frac{n}{2}\right) \right] + nT(n)≤2[c(2n​)log2​(2n​)]+n
  • Simplify the constant factor: T(n)≤cnlog⁡2(n2)+nT(n) \le c n \log_2\left(\frac{n}{2}\right) + nT(n)≤cnlog2​(2n​)+n
  • Apply logarithm quotient rule log⁡2(n/2)=log⁡2n−log⁡22\log_2(n/2) = \log_2 n - \log_2 2log2​(n/2)=log2​n−log2​2: T(n)≤cn(log⁡2n−1)+nT(n) \le c n (\log_2 n - 1) + nT(n)≤cn(log2​n−1)+n
  • Expand the bracket: T(n)≤cnlog⁡2n−cn+nT(n) \le c n \log_2 n - c n + nT(n)≤cnlog2​n−cn+n
  • Factor out nnn: T(n)≤cnlog⁡2n−(c−1)nT(n) \le c n \log_2 n - (c - 1)nT(n)≤cnlog2​n−(c−1)n
  • For the bound T(n)≤cnlog⁡2nT(n) \le c n \log_2 nT(n)≤cnlog2​n to hold, we need: −(c−1)n≤0-(c - 1)n \le 0−(c−1)n≤0 c−1≥0c - 1 \ge 0c−1≥0 c≥1c \ge 1c≥1

1.3.4 Base Case Verification​

  • Choose n=2n = 2n=2: T(2)=2T(1)+2=2(1)+2=4T(2) = 2T(1) + 2 = 2(1) + 2 = 4T(2)=2T(1)+2=2(1)+2=4
  • Check against bound: c⋅2log⁡22=2cc \cdot 2 \log_2 2 = 2cc⋅2log2​2=2c
  • Requirement: 4≤2c  ⟹  c≥24 \le 2c \implies c \ge 24≤2c⟹c≥2
  • Choosing c=2c = 2c=2 satisfies both the base case and the inductive step.
  • Conclusion: T(n)=O(nlog⁡n)T(n) = \mathbf{O(n \log n)}T(n)=O(nlogn)

Unit - 2

Divide & Conquer Algorithms​

2.1 Binary Search​

2.1.1 Concept​

  • Works on sorted arrays by repeatedly comparing the target key with the middle element.
  • If key matches, index is returned.
  • If key is smaller, search space reduces to left half.
  • If key is greater, search space reduces to right half.

2.1.2 Numerical Problem​

  • Sorted array: A=[11,22,33,44,55,66,77,88,99]A = [11, 22, 33, 44, 55, 66, 77, 88, 99]A=[11,22,33,44,55,66,77,88,99]
  • Indices: 000 to 888
  • Target key: Key=66\text{Key} = 66Key=66

2.1.3 Iteration-by-Iteration Trace​

Iteration 1​
  • Lower pointer: low=0\text{low} = 0low=0
  • Upper pointer: high=8\text{high} = 8high=8
  • Calculate mid: mid=⌊0+82⌋=4\text{mid} = \left\lfloor \frac{0 + 8}{2} \right\rfloor = 4mid=⌊20+8​⌋=4
  • Inspect element: A[4]=55A[4] = 55A[4]=55
  • Compare: 66>5566 > 5566>55
  • Action:
    • Target lies in the right half.
    • Update: low=mid+1=4+1=5\text{low} = \text{mid} + 1 = 4 + 1 = 5low=mid+1=4+1=5
Iteration 2​
  • Lower pointer: low=5\text{low} = 5low=5
  • Upper pointer: high=8\text{high} = 8high=8
  • Calculate mid: mid=⌊5+82⌋=⌊6.5⌋=6\text{mid} = \left\lfloor \frac{5 + 8}{2} \right\rfloor = \lfloor 6.5 \rfloor = 6mid=⌊25+8​⌋=⌊6.5⌋=6
  • Inspect element: A[6]=66A[6] = 66A[6]=66
  • Compare: 66==6666 == 6666==66
  • Action:
    • Match found at index 666.
    • Search terminates.

2.1.4 Complexity​

  • Comparisons made: 222
  • Time Complexity:
    • Best Case: O(1)O(1)O(1)
    • Average Case: O(log⁡n)O(\log n)O(logn)
    • Worst Case: O(log⁡n)\mathbf{O(\log n)}O(logn)
  • Space Complexity: O(1)\mathbf{O(1)}O(1) (Iterative).

2.2 Merge Sort​

2.2.1 Concept​

  • Follows the Divide, Conquer, and Combine paradigm:
    • Divide: Split array into two halves at midpoint.
    • Conquer: Recursively sort both subarrays.
    • Combine: Merge the two sorted subarrays using two pointers.

2.2.2 Numerical Problem​

  • Input array: A=[38,27,43,3,9,82,10]A = [38, 27, 43, 3, 9, 82, 10]A=[38,27,43,3,9,82,10]
  • Size: n=7n = 7n=7

  • Level 0: [38,27,43,3,9,82,10][38, 27, 43, 3, 9, 82, 10][38,27,43,3,9,82,10]
  • Level 1:
    • Left: [38,27,43,3][38, 27, 43, 3][38,27,43,3]
    • Right: [9,82,10][9, 82, 10][9,82,10]
  • Level 2:
    • From Left: [38,27][38, 27][38,27] and [43,3][43, 3][43,3]
    • From Right: [9][9][9] and [82,10][82, 10][82,10]
  • Level 3 (Base Cases):
    • [38],[27],[43],[3],[9],[82],[10][38], [27], [43], [3], [9], [82], [10][38],[27],[43],[3],[9],[82],[10]

2.2.4 Conquer & Merge Step​

Sub-Merge 1​

    • Compare 383838 and 27  ⟹  27<3827 \implies 27 < 3827⟹27<38
    • Result: [27,38][27, 38][27,38]
Sub-Merge 2​
  • Merge [43][43][43] and [3][3][3]:
    • Compare 434343 and 3  ⟹  3<433 \implies 3 < 433⟹3<43
    • Result: [3,43][3, 43][3,43]
Sub-Merge 3​
  • Merge [27,38][27, 38][27,38] and [3,43][3, 43][3,43]:
    • Compare 272727 and 3  ⟹  3 \implies3⟹ Take 333
    • Compare 272727 and 43  ⟹  43 \implies43⟹ Take 272727
    • Compare 383838 and 43  ⟹  43 \implies43⟹ Take 383838
    • Remaining: Take 434343
    • Result: [3,27,38,43][3, 27, 38, 43][3,27,38,43]
Sub-Merge 4​
  • Merge [82][82][82] and [10][10][10]:
    • Compare 828282 and 10  ⟹  10 \implies10⟹ Take 101010
    • Result: [10,82][10, 82][10,82]
Sub-Merge 5​
  • Merge [9][9][9] and [10,82][10, 82][10,82]:

Final Merge Step​

    • Compare 272727 and 10  ⟹  10 \implies10⟹ Output 101010

2.3 Quick Sort (Lomuto Partitioning)​

2.3.1 Concept & Partition Logic​

  • Chooses the last element as the pivot: P=A[high]P = A[\text{high}]P=A[high].

2.4 Strassen's Matrix Multiplication (2×22 \times 22×2)​

  • Standard multiplication uses 888 scalar multiplications.
  • Strassen uses 777 products, saving computational overhead on large matrices.

    • b21=4b_{21} = 4b21​=4
    • b22=2b_{22} = 2b22​=2

2.4.3 The 7 Auxiliary Products (P1P_1P1​ to P7P_7P7​)​

  • Product P3P_3P3​: P3=a11(b12−b22)P_3 = a_{11} (b_{12} - b_{22})P3​=a11​(b12​−b22​) P3=1×(8−2)P_3 = 1 \times (8 - 2)P3​=1×(8−2) P3=1×6P_3 = 1 \times 6P3​=1×6 P3=6P_3 = 6P3​=6

  • Product P4P_4P4​: P4=a22(b21−b11)P_4 = a_{22} (b_{21} - b_{11})P4​=a22​(b21​−b11​) P4=5×(4−6)P_4 = 5 \times (4 - 6)P4​=5×(4−6) P4=5×(−2)P_4 = 5 \times (-2)P4​=5×(−2) P4=−10P_4 = -10P4​=−10

  • Product P6P_6P6​: P6=(a21−a11)(b11+b12)P_6 = (a_{21} - a_{11})(b_{11} + b_{12})P6​=(a21​−a11​)(b11​+b12​) P6=(7−1)(6+8)P_6 = (7 - 1)(6 + 8)P6​=(7−1)(6+8) P6=6×14P_6 = 6 \times 14P6​=6×14 P6=84P_6 = 84P6​=84

2.5 Divide and Conquer Modular Exponentiation​

2.5.1 Recursive Exponentiation Rule​

  • For base aaa and exponent nnn:
    • If n==0n == 0n==0: a0=1a^0 = 1a0=1
    • If nnn is even: an=(an/2)2a^n = (a^{n/2})^2an=(an/2)2
    • If nnn is odd: an=a×(a(n−1)/2)2a^n = a \times (a^{(n-1)/2})^2an=a×(a(n−1)/2)2

2.5.2 Numerical Problem​

  • Compute: 310(mod1000)3^{10} \pmod{1000}310(mod1000)

2.5.3 Step-by-Step Computation​

  • Step 1: Break down 3103^{10}310 (even power): 310=(35)23^{10} = (3^5)^2310=(35)2
  • Step 2: Break down 353^535 (odd power): 35=3×(32)23^5 = 3 \times (3^2)^235=3×(32)2
  • Step 3: Compute 323^232: 32=93^2 = 932=9
  • Step 4: Compute (32)2(3^2)^2(32)2: 92=819^2 = 8192=81
  • Step 5: Compute 353^535: 35=3×81=2433^5 = 3 \times 81 = 24335=3×81=243
  • Step 6: Compute 3103^{10}310: 310=2432=59,0493^{10} = 243^2 = 59,049310=2432=59,049
  • Step 7: Apply modulo 100010001000: 59,049(mod1000)=4959,049 \pmod{1000} = \mathbf{49}59,049(mod1000)=49

2.5.4 Complexity Comparison​

  • Sequential multiplication multiplications: 999 multiplications
  • Divide and conquer multiplications: 444 multiplications
  • Time Complexity: O(log⁡n)\mathbf{O(\log n)}O(logn)

7.2 Rabin-Karp Algorithm (Rolling Hash)​

7.2.1 Problem Parameters​

  • Text: T="31415926535"T = \text{"31415926535"}T="31415926535"
  • Pattern: P="26"P = \text{"26"}P="26"
  • Pattern length: m=2m = 2m=2
  • Radix / Base: d=10d = 10d=10
  • Prime modulus: q=11q = 11q=11
  • High-order multiplier: h=dm−1(modq)=102−1(mod11)=10h = d^{m-1} \pmod q = 10^{2-1} \pmod{11} = 10h=dm−1(modq)=102−1(mod11)=10

7.2.2 Pattern Hash Calculation​

  • Direct value: 262626
  • Hash: p=26(mod11)=4p = 26 \pmod{11} = \mathbf{4}p=26(mod11)=4

7.2.3 Window-by-Window Rolling Hash Trace​

  • Window 0 ("31"): t0=31(mod11)=9≠4t_0 = 31 \pmod{11} = 9 \ne 4t0​=31(mod11)=9=4
  • Window 1 ("14"): t1=14(mod11)=3≠4t_1 = 14 \pmod{11} = 3 \ne 4t1​=14(mod11)=3=4
  • Window 2 ("41"): t2=41(mod11)=8≠4t_2 = 41 \pmod{11} = 8 \ne 4t2​=41(mod11)=8=4
  • Window 3 ("15"): t3=15(mod11)=4==pt_3 = 15 \pmod{11} = 4 == pt3​=15(mod11)=4==p
    • Hash match! Verify characters:
    • String "15" ≠\ne= "26"
    • Spurious Hit!
  • Window 4 ("59"): t4=59(mod11)=4==pt_4 = 59 \pmod{11} = 4 == pt4​=59(mod11)=4==p
    • Hash match! String "59" ≠\ne= "26"
    • Spurious Hit!
  • Window 5 ("92"): t5=92(mod11)=4==pt_5 = 92 \pmod{11} = 4 == pt5​=92(mod11)=4==p
    • Hash match! String "92" ≠\ne= "26"
    • Spurious Hit!
  • Window 6 ("26"): t6=26(mod11)=4==pt_6 = 26 \pmod{11} = 4 == pt6​=26(mod11)=4==p
    • Hash match! Verify characters:
    • String "26" ====== "26"
    • Valid Match found at Shift 666!

7.2.4 Rolling Hash Formula Calculation Step-by-Step​

  • Shift formula: ts+1=(d(ts−T[s+1]⋅h)+T[s+m+1])(modq)t_{s+1} = \left( d (t_s - T[s+1] \cdot h) + T[s+m+1] \right) \pmod qts+1​=(d(ts​−T[s+1]⋅h)+T[s+m+1])(modq)
  • Example: Transition from Window 0 ("31") to Window 1 ("14"):
    • Outgoing digit: 333
    • Incoming digit: 444
    • Calculation: t1=(10(31−3×10)+4)(mod11)t_1 = (10(31 - 3 \times 10) + 4) \pmod{11}t1​=(10(31−3×10)+4)(mod11) t1=(10(1)+4)(mod11)=14(mod11)=3t_1 = (10(1) + 4) \pmod{11} = 14 \pmod{11} = 3t1​=(10(1)+4)(mod11)=14(mod11)=3
  • Time Complexity:
    • Average Case: O(n+m)\mathbf{O(n + m)}O(n+m)
    • Worst Case: O((n−m+1)m)\mathbf{O((n - m + 1)m)}O((n−m+1)m)

    • On ′b′'b'′b′: Suffix of "abb" is ∅  ⟹  \emptyset \implies∅⟹ State 000.
  • From State 333 ("aba"):

7.5 NP-Completeness Foundations & Polynomial-Time Reduction​

7.5.1 Definitions: P, NP, NP-Hard, NP-Complete​

  • Class P: Problems solvable in polynomial time (O(nk)O(n^k)O(nk)).
  • Class NP: Decision problems whose solutions are verifiable in polynomial time.
  • NP-Hard: Problems at least as hard as any problem in NP (not necessarily in NP).
  • NP-Complete: Problems that are both in NP and NP-Hard.

7.5.2 3-SAT to CLIQUE Reduction Example​

  • 3-CNF Boolean formula ϕ\phiϕ with kkk clauses: ϕ=(x1∨¬x2∨x3)∧(¬x1∨x2∨x4)\phi = (x_1 \lor \neg x_2 \lor x_3) \land (\neg x_1 \lor x_2 \lor x_4)ϕ=(x1​∨¬x2​∨x3​)∧(¬x1​∨x2​∨x4​)
  • Number of clauses: k=2k = 2k=2

7.5.3 Visual Reduction Graph Diagram​

7.5.4 Graph Transformation Step-by-Step​

  • Clause 1: create vertices for literals v1,1(x1),v1,2(¬x2),v1,3(x3)v_{1,1}(x_1), v_{1,2}(\neg x_2), v_{1,3}(x_3)v1,1​(x1​),v1,2​(¬x2​),v1,3​(x3​).
  • Clause 2: create vertices for literals v2,1(¬x1),v2,2(x2),v2,3(x4)v_{2,1}(\neg x_1), v_{2,2}(x_2), v_{2,3}(x_4)v2,1​(¬x1​),v2,2​(x2​),v2,3​(x4​).
  • Edge placement rule:
    • Connect two vertices if they are in different clauses AND are not complementary (i.e. not xix_ixi​ and ¬xi\neg x_i¬xi​).

7.5.5 Equivalence Proof Walkthrough​

  • If ϕ\phiϕ is satisfiable:
    • Choosing assignment x1=True,x2=Truex_1 = \text{True}, x_2 = \text{True}x1​=True,x2​=True:
    • Literal x1x_1x1​ in Clause 1 is True.
    • Literal x2x_2x2​ in Clause 2 is True.
    • They are in different clauses and not contradictory.
    • An edge exists between them, forming a Clique of size k=2k = 2k=2.
  • If graph has a kkk-clique:
    • Exactly one vertex per clause is chosen.
    • Since no edges exist between contradictory literals, setting all selected literals to True satisfies formula ϕ\phiϕ.
  • Proves 3-SAT≤PCLIQUE\text{3-SAT} \le_P \text{CLIQUE}3-SAT≤P​CLIQUE.
